To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the attenuation of laser light following the termination of cryogen spray cooling (i.e. the time when the laser light is incident upon a dry skin surface) is dependent upon the cryogen film thickness, the laser pulse energy, and the laser pulse duration.

cryogen spray cooling (1) attenuates laser light in a wavelength‐dependent manner; (2) the degree of light attenuation is proportional to cryogen film thickness; and (3) light attenuation can be reduced by increasing the laser pulse duration.

(1) the laser light attenuation following CSC spurt termination was found to be dependent on the laser wavelength, (2) the attenuation was also found to depend on the CSC spurt length, (3) the attenuation was found to be higher for longer pulse durations and (4) the attenuation was not found to depend on pulse energy.

the measurement of the laser light attenuation due the cryogen spurt termination.
the measurement of the attenuation of laser light by a cryogen spray cooling film on the skin.
the measurement of laser light attenuation in the presence of cryogen spray cooling.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there is no evidence that the laser light is attenuated by the cryogen film.
there is no evidence that the cryogen film causes significant laser light attenuation.
cryogen spray cooling is a safe and effective method for reducing the risk of epidemal injury during laser surgery.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the cryogen spray cooling (spurt) termination does not cause significant attenuation of the laser light.
the laser light attenuation is minimal and is not a significant factor to consider during the application of CSC.
the attenuation of the light is minimal.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the optical attenuation of laser light by the cryogen film is negligible.
the attenuation of laser light due to optical scattering from the CSC spurt is not significant and can be neglected in the context of laser dermatological surgery.
the attenuation of light following the termination of a CSC spurt is not a major concern for laser dermatological surgery.
